title: Two Gaussian covariance models fail residual checks in 176 IBL brain regions
abstract: We tested whether a joint covariance model can split regional physiology into wiring, cell-type, spatial and noise shares. We used five task scores and nine spike measures in 176 IBL regions, with Knox input wiring, Allen MERFISH supertypes and CCF centroids. We removed means for 12 anatomical divisions. A matrix-normal model allowed an unrestricted feature covariance in each family. In 199 refitted simulations per fit, both task and intrinsic residuals had more variation across regions and larger extremes than the model predicted. Each check had Monte Carlo p=0.005 and Holm p=0.030 within its six-test set. An exploratory inverse-session noise kernel reduced fitted wiring weight from 0.279 to 0.228 for task coding and from 0.250 to 0.149 for intrinsic spiking. Both extended fits still failed these residual checks. Cell-type weights were near zero for task coding and 0.307 to 0.329 for intrinsic spiking. These weights retain the earlier qualitative pattern but do not give a trusted biological variance split. The failure can reflect sampling error, heavy tails or an incorrect shared covariance form. No causal fraction is identified. Code, source hashes, aggregate fits, simulation draws and figures are supplied. External source tables and record-level derivatives are regenerated outside the package.
